answer.answer:
Yes, a married Singapore Citizen can buy an HDB flat with a Singapore PR spouse as an SC/SPR household.[1][2]

The sources I have do not state a blanket rule that such a couple can buy a new flat in every case, but they do show that married couples and/or parents with children can buy as an SC or SPR household, and that any buyer and core family nucleus member who is an SPR must have held SPR status for at least 3 years at the time of the HFE letter application.[1][2]

You should also note the property ownership rules. For buying a flat from HDB, all applicants and occupiers in the HFE application must not own or have an interest in any local or overseas private residential property, and must not have disposed of any such property within 30 months before the HFE letter application.[1]

HDB also requires you to apply for an HFE letter first, which will confirm your eligibility to buy a new or resale flat.[3] Please check the linked official page for the latest position before applying.

answer.answer:
At age 60, you may have a few possible HDB options, but whether a 3-room flat is available depends on whether you are buying alone or with someone else. If you are buying alone as a Singapore citizen, the Singles scheme says singles aged 35 and above can buy a flat on their own, and you should apply for an HDB Flat Eligibility (HFE) letter first to confirm what you can buy, what grants you may get, and whether you qualify for an HDB loan [2].

For people aged 55 and above, CPF’s guide says you can buy a short-lease 2-room Flexi flat, or any flat in the resale market [4]. If you are considering an HDB loan, HDB says a housing loan is not available for 2-room Flexi flats on short lease or Community Care Apartments; these must be paid using cash and/or CPF Ordinary Account savings [1].

If you are buying with family, spouse, or a non-resident spouse, different rules may apply, and HDB points buyers in those situations to the Couples and Families route instead [2][5].

To narrow this down, I’d need to know:
1. Are you buying alone, with a spouse, or with family?
2. Are you looking at a new flat or a resale flat?
3. Do you mean a 3-room resale flat, or a new 3-room flat from HDB?
4. Will you need an HDB loan, bank loan, or use cash/CPF only?

Also, for resale flats, HDB says you should check financing, lease-related CPF/loan restrictions, and get your HFE letter before proceeding [6]. Please check the linked official pages for the latest position [2][5][6].

A first-time married couple buying an HDB resale flat may qualify for the Family Grant, if at least 1 core member is a first-timer and the first-timer core applicant and/or occupier has not taken any housing subsidy before.[2]

They may also qualify for the Top-Up Grant only in a specific situation: if one of them had previously received a Singles Grant or bought a 2-room Flexi flat from HDB as a single, with other single citizens, or with a non-resident spouse, and has not taken any other housing subsidy apart from that.[2]

I couldn't confirm from the official sources I have whether a first-time married couple may also qualify for the Enhanced CPF Housing Grant or Proximity Housing Grant, because the passages provided here only cover the singles versions of those grants, not the family rules.[3][4]

HDB says you should apply for an HDB Flat Eligibility (HFE) letter through the HDB Flat Portal, as it will show your eligibility to buy a resale flat and the CPF housing grants you are eligible for.[1] Please check the linked official page for the latest position.

answer.answer:
A first-time married couple buying an HDB resale flat may qualify for these grants, if they meet the eligibility conditions:

- **Family Grant** under the CPF Housing Grant Scheme for families buying a resale flat. HDB says this can be **up to $80,000**. It is for couples/families who are first-timer applicants buying an HDB resale flat, and at least 1 core member must be a first-timer for the grant. First-timer core applicants and/or occupiers must not have taken any housing subsidy before. [2]

- **Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG) for Families**. If you are a first-timer applicant, you may be eligible for the EHG for a new or resale flat. **From 20 August 2024**, first-timer families may qualify for **up to $120,000**. For a resale flat, you must first qualify for the resale **Family Grant** before you may be eligible for the EHG. [1]

- **Proximity Housing Grant (PHG)**. HDB says families buying a resale flat may also apply for the PHG if they meet its eligibility conditions. [1][2]

- **Top-Up Grant**, in a special case: if one spouse had previously taken the **Singles Grant** for a resale flat or bought a **2-room or 2-room Flexi flat** from HDB as a single and is now married, they may apply for the Top-Up Grant. [2]

For the latest conditions, check the linked HDB pages, as details can change. [1][2]

Plan for both cash and CPF at different stages of the resale purchase; HDB says you should ensure you have sufficient funds for all required payments.[2]

The buyer who is not taking any housing loans must indicate that he is financing the flat purchase fully with his CPF savings and/or cash when he submits the resale application to HDB.

**28 ADDITIONAL BUYER’S STAMP DUTY**

The buyer must pay the prevailing stamp duties relating to the purchase of the flat (including but not limited to Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty) as may be imposed by the Government from time to time. Where the buyer needs to pay part of such stamp duties in cash, the buyer shall pay to HDB upon HDB's request after the acceptance of the resale application, within the timeframe specified by HDB and in any mode of payment that HDB may decide, failing which HDB reserves the right not to approve the resale.

**29 AFTER RESALE COMPLETION**

29.1 The buyer shall pay all rates, taxes and charges imposed on the flat after the resale completion date.

29.2 The buyer shall not transfer, assign, mortgage, charge, rent out or part with the possession of the flat or any part of the flat without the prior written consent of HDB.

29.3 The buyer shall keep in good and tenantable repair and condition the interior of the flat including all fixtures and fittings.

29.4 The buyer shall notify HDB and obtain its prior written consent from the respective HDB Branch before making any alterations or additions to the flat.

answer.answer:
Plan for these upfront items when buying an HDB resale flat:

- OTP deposit to the seller: total $2 to $5,000, made up of the Option Fee and Option Exercise Fee. The Option Fee is $1 to $1,000 when the OTP is granted, and the Option Exercise Fee is the balance so that the total does not exceed $5,000. This forms part of the resale price. [2][3]
- Resale application fee: $80, or $40 for 1- and 2-room flats, when you submit your portion of the resale application. [2]
- Request for Value fee: $120 if you intend to use CPF savings and/or a housing loan, unless otherwise advised by the financial institution. [2]
- Legal fees: payable, but the amount depends on the solicitor you appoint. [2]
- Initial payment: you may use CPF savings for the initial payment. If you take a housing loan from a financial institution, at least 5% of the initial payment must be in cash. For a bank/FI loan, the remaining 20% of the downpayment can be paid using CPF savings. [1][2]
- Balance purchase price: any amount not covered by the initial payment, CPF housing grants, CPF OA savings and eligible housing loan must be paid before or during completion. [2]
- Stamp duties: you must pay the prevailing stamp duties, and if part must be paid in cash, HDB will request it after accepting the resale application. [4]

CPF housing grants, if eligible, can be used for the initial payment and to reduce the loan amount. Check the latest official pages, as rules may change. [2]

6.1 If there is a recess area space fronting the flat available for sale, the buyers may request HDB to process the application to buy the recess area together with the resale application. How much CPF savings you can use for your home purchase

Learn more about the amount of CPF OA savings you can use to purchase a home.

*4 Aug 2025*

*SOURCE: CPF Board*

There is a limit on how much of your CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings can be used for a home purchase. This is so that you would have enough for your retirement.

This limit differs based on the valuation of the flat at time of purchase, purchase price, type of property, loan type, and age of property.

If the remaining lease of the flat can last the youngest owner until age 95, the amount of CPF savings you can use is capped at the lower of the purchase price and the valuation price at the time of purchase.

Your CPF savings can be used for purchasing a home, but did you know that there are limits in place?

Read on to learn more about using your CPF savings for a home purchase.

Part/Chapter: Part B

1. Use of CPF savings

a. You may use your CPF Ordinary Account (“**OA**”) savings for the following:

i. Direct payment of the purchase price of your private residential property to the property developer or sellers;

ii. Repayment of the housing loan in part or whole and/or to pay the monthly instalment of the housing loan taken for the purchase of your property, land and/or for construction of a house on that land; and/or

iii. Payment of the stamp duty, legal fees and other related costs incurred by you in connection with the purchase or mortgage of the property and/or construction of the house.

b. CPF savings cannot be used for the following:

i. Payment of option fees to property developers or sellers;

ii. Payment of construction works, improvements, repairs and/or renovation of your private residential property;

iii. Payment of monthly service and conservancy charges including all rates, taxes and other charges imposed on your private residential property;

iv. Repayment of non-housing loans (i.e. loans not taken for the purchase of your private residential property) and miscellaneous cost (i.e. penalties, insurance charges); or

v. Payment of purchase price that is above the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for resale private residential property; and/or

vi. Reimbursement of any payments made to the property developers or sellers out of your personal funds in respect of the purchase of your private residential property.

answer.answer:
Yes. CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings can be used to pay stamp duty and legal fees when buying a home under the CPF Housing Scheme.[1]

CPF says OA savings may be used for the home purchase, downpayment, housing loan, and also “stamp and legal fees”.[1] For private residential properties, the terms also state that OA savings may be used for “payment of the stamp duty, legal fees and other related costs” connected with the purchase or mortgage of the property and/or construction of the house.[3]

But there are limits on how much OA you can use for a property purchase. The amount depends on factors such as the remaining lease, property type and loan type.[2] CPF also says there are housing usage limits, so you should check the official CPF housing usage calculator and the latest CPF page for your exact case.[1][2]

Section: FAQs

The amount of CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings you can use depends on:

Remaining lease of the property

Type of property

Note: For members age 55 and above, your Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) is [half of your Full Retirement Sum](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/article/how-much-is-my-basic-retirement-sum) (FRS) which depends on the year you turn 55 and will remain the same for life. For members below 55, your BRS is half of the prevailing FRS in the year.

You can use our [CPF Housing Usage Calculator](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/cpf-housing-usage) to determine the total amount of CPF savings that you and your co-owner (if any) may use to buy your property.

CPF savings used to pay for stamp duty, legal fees and upgrading costs are not included in the CPF housing limit.

Purchasing your second or subsequent property

Yes, but only up to the CPF housing limit for your flat or property. The use of CPF for housing is subject to CPF housing limits, for both HDB/DBSS flats and private residential properties.[1]

Once that limit is reached, you cannot keep using CPF for the balance purchase price or monthly housing loan instalments. HDB states that after the CPF limit is reached, you “will not be able to withdraw more of your CPF savings” and will have to pay the balance flat purchase price and/or monthly mortgage instalments in cash.[4]

The exact limit depends on factors such as whether it is an HDB/DBSS flat or private property, when it was bought, and the remaining lease at the time of purchase.[1] For some cases, no CPF can be used at all if the remaining lease was 20 years or less at the time of purchase.[1]

So the direct answer is: no, you cannot continue paying your housing loan with CPF after reaching the applicable withdrawal limit.[4] Check the latest official CPF/HDB page for your property type and purchase date, as the applicable limit depends on those details.[1]

answer.answer:
Home Protection Scheme (HPS) is meant to protect HDB flat owners and their families against losing the home if the insured person dies, becomes terminally ill, or suffers total permanent disability.[1]

From the official source I have, I could confirm one key exception: you can apply for exemption from HPS if you already have equivalent life insurance coverage.[1] The listed policies are Whole Life, Term Life, Endowments, Life Riders attached to a basic policy, and Mortgage Reducing Term Assurance / Decreasing Term Rider.[1]

To qualify for that exemption, the policy must cover your outstanding housing loan for the full loan term or until age 65, whichever is earlier.[1]

I couldn't find a fuller official rule in the passages provided on exactly who must have HPS in every situation, or any other exceptions beyond exemption based on equivalent life insurance. You may want to check the linked CPF page for the latest position.[1]

Apply for HPS first before getting exemption

Doing so will avoid any delay in commencing the use of your CPF savings for your monthly housing instalments.

You can apply for HPS exemption after you have obtained legal ownership of the flat and the housing loan for the property has been disbursed.

If you have not previously used your CPF savings for your HDB flat at the time of purchase or for your monthly housing instalment, please fill up this [application form](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/hdbbankloan) to start using your CPF savings for your HDB flat.

Please approach the insurer(s) of your private insurance policy(s) to submit your application to be exempted from HPS. We will only process applications submitted through insurers.

You will need to provide your insurer(s) with supporting documents showing your current* housing loan details, i.e. loan commencement date, balance loan amount, balance term of loan & the mortgage rate. These can generally be found on your housing loan statement.

*Within 6 months from the date the application for exemption is submitted.

If you are covered under HPS and we receive your HPS exemption request from your insurer within one month of the issuance of your HPS cover, we will refund the full premium into your Ordinary Account. Otherwise, you will receive a pro-rated premium refund upon the termination of your HPS cover.

Home Protection Scheme (HPS) is for CPF members who own an HDB flat and are paying their monthly housing instalments using CPF savings or cash. It covers them until age 65, or until the housing loan is fully paid, whichever is earlier. If the loan will only be fully paid after age 65, CPF says to consider private insurance after HPS ends at 65.[1]

This applies when you are using CPF savings for monthly housing instalments, whether you are taking an HDB loan or a bank loan.[1]

The key exception is that you can apply to be exempted from HPS if you already have equivalent private life insurance.[1] The accepted policy types include whole life, term life, endowment, life riders attached to a basic policy, and MRTA/decreasing term rider policies.[1] These policies must cover your outstanding housing loan for the full loan term or until age 65, whichever is earlier.[1]

For the exemption process, you should first apply for HPS to avoid delays in using CPF savings for monthly instalments. You can apply for exemption only after you have legal ownership of the flat and the housing loan has been disbursed, and the application must be submitted through your insurer with current loan details.[1]

Please check the linked CPF page for the latest position.[1]

Section: Terms and conditions for use of CPF under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Application of terms and conditions > Part C - Standard terms and conditions > 2. Use of CPF saving for Multiple Property purchase
Part/Chapter: Part C

2. Use of CPF saving for Multiple Property purchase

a. There are additional restrictions if you have used your CPF savings for a property and are applying to use your CPF savings for a second or subsequent property (“**Multiple Property**”).

b. For Multiple Property bought from 1 July 2006 but before 10 May 2019:

i. You are required to set aside the latest BRS before you can use the excess savings in your OA for the Multiple Property;

ii. The maximum amount of CPF that can be used for your Multiple Property is capped at:

• Lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for property with a remaining lease of at least 60 years at the time of purchase; or

• A percentage of the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for property with a remaining lease of less than 60 years but at least 30 years at the time of purchase.

c. For Multiple Property bought from 10 May 2019:

i. You are required to set aside the following before you can use the excess savings in your OA for the Multiple Property

• The latest BRS if you have at least one property bought using CPF or the property that you are buying can cover you till age 95*

• The latest Full Retirement Sum (“FRS”) if you do not have any property that can cover you till age 95

* If you subsequently sell the property that can cover you till age 95, you will need to set aside the FRS instead.

The key CPF restriction is this: for a second or subsequent property, you can use OA savings only after setting aside the required retirement sum, and the amount depends on whether you have a property that can cover you till age 95. If you buy from 10 May 2019, you must set aside the latest BRS if you already have at least one property bought using CPF, or if the property you are buying can cover you till age 95; otherwise you must set aside the latest FRS. evidence.title: CPFB | How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
evidence.text:
Document: CPFB | How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
Section: FAQs

To check the exact amount that you need to refund your CPF accounts if you sell/transfer your property, simply log in to your [Home ownership dashboard](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/homeownershipdashboard) and look under the “What Happens If” section.

In general, the amount you must refund is the principal you have withdrawn for your property (P) and the accrued interest (I), i.e. “P+I”. If you are age 55 or above and have pledged your property to set aside your retirement sum, you must also refund the pledged amount.

**IMPORTANT NOTE:**

However, please note that your required CPF refund is less than your P+I if you:

were age 55 or older before 1 January 2013; and

have set aside your Full Retirement Sum (FRS) before 1 January 2013.

This is because having set aside your FRS before 1 January 2013, you are not required by law to refund the CPF you have used to pay for your property prior to 2013. If you have continued to use your CPF from 1 January 2013, only the principal amount used from 1 January 2013 and the accrued interest need to be refunded when you sell your property.

At age 58, the retirement-sum rules for members aged 55 and above apply. Your Basic Retirement Sum is half of your Full Retirement Sum, and your FRS depends on the year you turned 55 and stays the same for life [1]. You can check on the Retirement Dashboard whether you have already set aside your FRS [2].

Other CPF factors that affect how much you can use are: the property’s remaining lease, the type of property, the loan type, and whether it is your first or subsequent property [1]. CPF also says stamp duty, legal fees and upgrading costs are not counted within the CPF housing limit [1].

If you own a property in Singapore with a remaining lease that lasts you to age 95 or older, you may apply to withdraw RA savings down to your BRS [2].

If you are selling or transferring your current home, the missing fact that matters is your CPF refund amount. In general, you must refund the principal withdrawn plus accrued interest, and if you are 55 or above and pledged your property to set aside your retirement sum, you must also refund the pledged amount [3]. Check the linked official dashboards/calculator for your latest position [1][2][3].
